title: Collapse in the ED waiting area in a 75-year-old man
desc: This station involves a witnessed collapse of a 75-year-old man in the ED waiting area. The candidate runs a rapid DRSABCD assessment and advanced life support for a shockable arrest. After return of spontaneous circulation, they do a primary survey and take a collateral history from his wife. They then interpret his observations, post-resuscitation 12-lead ECG and blood gas, name the cause and the reversible causes of cardiac arrest, and outline post-resuscitation care, emergency reperfusion and communication with his family.
focus: In-hospital cardiac arrest: ANZCOR advanced life support for VF, finding the cause after ROSC, and post-resuscitation care with emergency PCI
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital that has a cardiac catheter laboratory. You are about to call your next patient from the waiting area when you see Phillip Smith, a 75-year-old man, collapse onto the floor. He came in with his wife, Helen, a short time ago, and she says he has been short of breath today.

Triage obtained a brief history:

  • Past history: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia.
  • Medicines: telmisartan, atorvastatin, metformin.
  • Social: ex-smoker, no alcohol, lives at home with his wife.

A nurse and other ED staff are close by and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Do a rapid assessment of Phillip and manage him, directing the team and telling the examiner what you are examining and doing. When it is safe, take a focused history from his wife, Helen, and complete a focused examination (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Phillip's observations, his post-resuscitation 12-lead ECG, and his blood and venous gas results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Roles: Phillip is unresponsive from the moment he collapses, so use a mannequin if you have one. The person playing the patient plays Helen Smith, his 72-year-old wife, and can also act as the nurse and the team. The examiner gives every finding from the Exam findings and the Resuscitation sequence below when the candidate says what they check or do. If the candidate asks for a 12-lead ECG, bloods or a gas, the nurse says it is done and the examiner says the results come in Part 2.

Opening line (Helen, kneeling beside him): "Phil! Phil! Somebody help, he's just gone down!"

Resuscitation sequence (examiner, compressing time)

  • Danger: if asked, a cup of water has spilled on the floor near his head (the rest of the floor is dry), a wheelchair is in the way, and there are no sharps. If the candidate asks, staff wipe up the water and move the wheelchair.
  • Response: there is no response to voice ("Can you hear me? Open your eyes. What is your name? Squeeze my hand") and no response to a trapezius squeeze, sternal rub or a shoulder squeeze.
  • Airway: no vomit, blood or foreign body in the mouth. With a jaw thrust or head tilt–chin lift the airway is open.
  • Breathing and pulse: no normal breathing (an occasional gasp only) and no carotid pulse. The collapse was at 10:08.
  • When the candidate calls for help, staff arrive with the arrest trolley and defibrillator. Resuscitation continues where he lies on the floor; if the candidate asks to move him, he is moved to the resus bay after ROSC. Staff do whatever role they are given.
  • Pads on, first rhythm check: show the rhythm strip (or read out): "The monitor shows chaotic, irregular deflections of varying amplitude. No P waves, QRS complexes or T waves can be seen." If the candidate checks for a pulse: none.
  • Each time the candidate calls for 2 minutes of CPR, say "Two minutes have passed, rhythm check due."
  • Rhythm checks 2, 3 and 4: the same rhythm, no pulse.
  • Rhythm check 5, after 4 shocks (about minute 6 of the station, whatever the candidate has given): "The monitor shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm at about 110. There is a carotid pulse." Return of spontaneous circulation is at 10:18.
  • If the candidate orders a drug, the nurse confirms it back ("Adrenaline 1 mg IV given") and the examiner notes the timing. The nurse does not prompt drugs or doses.
  • If the candidate asks for an advanced airway, the ED consultant agrees to do it once ROSC is achieved. Bag-valve-mask ventilation continues meanwhile.

Exam findings after ROSC (give only when asked)

  • Airway: patent with bag-valve-mask support (with an oropharyngeal airway in place if the candidate asked for one), no gag. He cannot protect his airway.
  • Breathing: irregular, inadequate spontaneous breaths about 6/min, so ventilation is assisted at 12/min. SpO2 97% on 15 L/min oxygen. Trachea central, chest rise equal, air entry equal on both sides, fine crackles at both bases. No surgical emphysema.
  • Circulation: HR 108 regular. Carotid and femoral pulses present. BP 96/60. CRT 4 seconds, cool peripheries. Heart sounds dual, not muffled, no murmur. JVP not seen (supine).
  • Disability: GCS 3 (E1 V1 M1). Pupils 3 mm, equal and sluggishly reactive. BGL 14.8 mmol/L.
  • Exposure: temperature 35.3 °C. No scalp haematoma or other injury from the fall. Abdomen soft. Calves soft and not swollen. No bleeding and no rash.
  • Triage observations, if the candidate asks the nurse (09:52): RR 24, SpO2 93% on room air, HR 104 regular, BP 148/86, temperature 36.6 °C, alert.

Helen's history (give only when asked)

  • Today: he woke at about 5:30 this morning "puffed" and has been short of breath all morning. It is worse when he moves, and he could not walk to the letterbox. He was clammy and sweaty and felt a bit sick. He rubbed his chest and said it felt "a bit tight", but he called it indigestion and did not want to come in. You brought him in at about 9:45.
  • Before today: no chest pain, heart attacks, palpitations, blackouts or heart tests. He has never had anything like this.
  • Other causes (say no if asked): no leg pain or swelling, no recent travel, operation or time in bed, no previous clots. No fever or cough. No vomiting or diarrhoea. No new tablets, and he could not have taken too many of anything. No kidney problems that you know of.
  • Medical history: type 2 diabetes for about 15 years, high blood pressure and high cholesterol, all managed by his GP.
  • Medicines: telmisartan, atorvastatin and metformin. No aspirin, no blood thinners. No allergies.
  • Bleeding risk (only if asked): no bleeding problems, no stroke, no stomach ulcers, no recent operations.
  • Social: smoked about 20 a day for 30 years and stopped 10 years ago. No alcohol. He is retired, independent and still drives. Lives with you at home.
  • Goals of care (only if asked): no advance care directive. "He'd want everything done. He's got a lot of living left."
  • He weighs about 88 kg.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are terrified. "Is it his heart? Is he going to die?" You feel guilty: "I should have made him come in this morning." You want to stay near him. If a staff member is asked to stay with you, you calm a little and answer questions clearly.

check.x: Professionalism

Checks for danger (spilled water near his head, which is wiped up before the pads go on; the wheelchair is moved; no sharps) and puts on gloves if they are at hand, without delaying assessment or CPR.
Leads as team leader: states the role, stays hands-off to direct, uses closed-loop communication and summarises to the team at each rhythm check.
Acknowledges Helen: asks a staff member to stay with her, offers her the choice to stay during the resuscitation, and speaks to her calmly in plain words.
History
Takes a collateral history of today's illness from Helen:
check.d: Credit if taken during CPR by the hands-off team leader or after ROSC.

kids.x: Breathlessness since waking at about 05:30, worse on exertion (could not walk to the letterbox)
Chest tightness he called indigestion, with sweating and nausea
No previous chest pain, heart problems, palpitations or blackouts

check.x: Screens for at least three other reversible causes: PE risk (leg swelling, travel, surgery or immobility), infection (fever or cough), fluid loss (vomiting or diarrhoea), new medicines or overdose, kidney disease.
Confirms medicines and allergies and checks it is safe to give antithrombotics: no aspirin or anticoagulant, no bleeding problems, stroke, peptic ulcer or recent surgery.
Asks about baseline function and goals of care: independent, no advance care directive, would want full active treatment (credit smoking history if asked).
Explores Helen's concerns: her fear that he will die, her guilt about not bringing him in sooner, and her wish to stay with him.
Examination
Assesses response (AVPU):

kids.x: To voice with clear commands (can you hear me, open your eyes, what is your name, squeeze my hand): no response
To touch or pain (firm shoulder squeeze; accept trapezius squeeze or sternal rub): no response

check.x: Sends for help:

kids.x: Presses the emergency buzzer, calls a Code Blue (arrest call) and asks for the defibrillator to be brought to him; applies the pads and analyses the rhythm where he lies; moves him to the resus bay only after ROSC (or when this will not delay defibrillation or interrupt CPR).
Allocates roles: airway, compressions (with a swap), defibrillation, IV access and medications, scribe

check.x: Assesses the airway for obstruction (vomit, blood, foreign body, swelling) and opens it with a jaw thrust (C-spine precautions after the fall) or a head tilt–chin lift, with suction ready.
Looks, listens and feels for breathing and checks the carotid pulse for no more than 10 seconds, then states that he is not breathing normally and has no pulse, so this is a cardiac arrest.
After ROSC, does a structured primary survey:

kids.x: Airway and breathing: airway protection (GCS 3, no gag), chest rise, trachea, breath sounds (bibasal crackles), SpO2
Circulation: pulse, BP, CRT and peripheral temperature, heart sounds (not muffled)
Disability: GCS, pupils and blood glucose
Exposure: temperature, injuries from the fall, calves

check.x: Interpretation
Identifies the monitor rhythm as ventricular fibrillation (chaotic irregular deflections of varying amplitude, no P waves, QRS complexes or T waves), a shockable rhythm.
check.d: Marked in Part 1 when the rhythm is shown.

check.x: Interprets the observations: abnormal before the arrest (RR 24, SpO2 93% on air), and after ROSC unresponsive with falling BP (96 to 82 systolic), rising HR (108 to 122) and longer CRT: post-arrest shock needing ICU now.
Reads the ECG as sinus tachycardia with ST elevation in V2 to V4, I, aVL, V5 and V6 and reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF: an anterolateral STEMI.

Notes the Q waves in V2 to V4, showing that the infarct has been evolving for hours (consistent with symptoms since 05:30), and names the left anterior descending artery, probably proximal, as the likely culprit.
Interprets the venous gas as a mixed respiratory (pCO2 58) and lactic metabolic acidosis (pH 7.12, lactate 8.6), with K 5.8 and glucose 14.8, the expected picture after an arrest.
Interprets the bloods: raised troponin fits but does not drive the decision; normal Hb, platelets and coagulation, so no bar to antithrombotics.
Gives the most likely diagnosis as a ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest caused by an acute anterolateral STEMI.
Names at least two reversible causes of cardiac arrest (4 Hs and 4 Ts), each with a feature for or against in Phillip.
check.d: For example: PE (no risk factors, calves normal), hyperkalaemia (5.8, explained by acidosis), tension pneumothorax or tamponade (equal air entry, heart sounds not muffled).

check.x: Management
Starts CPR straight away with correct technique:

kids.x: Heel of the hand on the lower half of the sternum, fingers interlocked, elbows straight
Rate 100 to 120/min, depth one third of the depth of the chest (accept about 5 cm), full recoil
30:2 with minimal interruptions, compressors swapping at rhythm checks

check.x: Ventilates with a bag-valve-mask and high-flow oxygen, watching the seal and chest rise. Sizes an oropharyngeal airway (corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw), uses suction, and asks for an advanced airway by a skilled operator, with waveform capnography once an advanced airway is placed.

Places the pads correctly (right infraclavicular and left mid-axillary at the V6 position, away from jewellery or a pacemaker). Defibrillates safely with COACHED, keeping compressions going while charging, then resumes CPR straight away for 2 minutes without a pulse check.
Asks for IV access with two large-bore cannulas (intraosseous if IV fails) and bloods including a venous gas, and considers the 4 Hs and 4 Ts during CPR.
Gives adrenaline 1 mg IV after the second shock, then every second loop (about every 4 minutes).
Gives amiodarone 300 mg IV after the third shock.
Recognises ROSC (an organised rhythm with a pulse) and asks for a 12-lead ECG straight away.
Activates the cath lab: phones the interventional cardiologist for immediate coronary angiography and PCI.

Gives nothing by mouth while the airway is unprotected; agrees aspirin (via orogastric tube once intubated, or IV if available) and heparin or other antithrombotics with the interventional cardiologist.
Outlines post-resuscitation care:

kids.x: Definitive airway; SpO2 94 to 98%; normocapnia confirmed on ABG/EtCO2
Vasopressor or inotrope for cardiogenic shock, target MAP 65 mmHg or above
Glucose 6 to 10 mmol/L avoiding hypoglycaemia; withhold metformin
Prevent fever (37.5 °C or below); do not rewarm

check.d: Credit any three of the four.

check.x: Refers to ICU for care after PCI and makes sure the scribe's record (times, rhythms, shocks, drugs) goes with him.
Safety netting
Makes the transfer safe: pads on, continuous monitoring, defibrillator and drugs go with him, airway-skilled escort; anticipates recurrent VF and worsening shock.

Explains to Helen in plain words: a heart attack made his heart stop, the team restarted it, and he now needs an urgent procedure to open the blocked artery. Says honestly that he is critically ill and it is too early to know about his recovery, including his brain. Says the delay was not her fault, invites questions and offers support (social worker).
Outlines follow-up: ICU post-arrest care, neurological prognosis not before 72 hours, echo and ICD assessment, cardiac rehabilitation.
check.d: Credit for naming any three of the four elements.

part2.lead: Phillip has a pulse and has been moved into the resus bay. Here are his observations, his post-resuscitation 12-lead ECG, and his blood and venous gas results.
part2.patient:
For question 4 only, the person playing Helen speaks to the candidate:

  • "What happened to him? Is he going to be all right?"
  • If the candidate explains in plain words, she asks: "Was it my fault? I should have brought him in this morning."
  • She calms if she is told honestly what is happening, that it was not her fault, and that someone will stay with her; she becomes more distressed if given jargon or false reassurance.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Triage set at 09:52. Cardiac arrest at 10:08, ROSC at 10:18. After ROSC, ventilation is assisted on 15 L/min oxygen, so the respiratory rate is the assisted rate. GCS 3.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage RR 24 and SpO2 93% on room air are yellow zone. HR 104, BP 148/86 and temperature are white. After ROSC (10:20) he is unresponsive (AVPU U, red zone), systolic BP is 96 (yellow), HR 108 (white), temperature 35.3 °C (yellow, mild post-arrest hypothermia), CRT 4 s, BGL 14.8, and SpO2 97% on 15 L. At 10:35 systolic BP is 82 (red), HR 122 (yellow), temperature 35.2 °C (yellow) and CRT 5 s.
  • Meaning: he was already hypoxic and tachypnoeic before the arrest, which fits LV failure from an evolving infarct. After ROSC he has falling BP, rising HR and poor perfusion: post-arrest shock, most likely cardiogenic.
  • Changes: red zone values call for a rapid response. The arrest team is already here, so ICU comes now. He needs a vasopressor or inotrope and an arterial line, and SpO2 97% on 15 L means the oxygen is titrated down to 94 to 98%. Do not actively rewarm; prevent fever.

rows.note: Triage: short of breath today; to waiting area
ROSC 10:18 after arrest at 10:08; ventilation assisted

handover.label: Post-resuscitation 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG: Phillip Smith, 75-year-old man, recorded at 10:22, 4 minutes after ROSC (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 108/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia, regular, with a P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +30°.
  • PR interval: 170 ms.
  • QRS: 100 ms. No bundle branch block. Q waves in V2 to V4, and small Q waves in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Poor R wave progression.
  • QTc: 460 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments: ST elevation of 3 to 4 mm in V2 to V4 and about 2 mm in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Reciprocal ST depression of about 1.5 mm in III and aVF. Lead II isoelectric.
  • T waves: upright in the leads with ST elevation, inverted in III and aVF.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG on file.
handover.model:
• Read: patient details and time (10:22, after ROSC). Sinus tachycardia at 108/min, normal axis, PR 170 ms, QRS 100 ms, QTc 460 ms. ST elevation in V2 to V4 and in the lateral leads I, aVL, V5 and V6, with reciprocal depression in III and aVF. Q waves are present, most prominent in V2 to V4. No old ECG for comparison.
  • Meaning: an anterolateral STEMI, most likely a proximal left anterior descending occlusion. The Q waves show the infarct has been evolving for hours, which fits breathlessness and chest tightness since 05:30. This is the cause of the VF arrest. Reciprocal change, Q waves and the history make a true STEMI far more likely than post-shock ST change.
  • Changes: emergency coronary angiography and PCI now, without waiting for the troponin. Repeat the 12-lead about 10 minutes after ROSC and after any rhythm change, but do not delay cath lab activation.

handover.label: Bloods and venous gas
handover.result: Venous samples taken from the IV cannula at 10:24, 6 minutes after ROSC, on 15 L/min oxygen with assisted ventilation. The group and hold sample was received and processed.
handover.model:
• Read: pH 7.12 with pCO2 58 and bicarbonate 18, base excess -10 and lactate 8.6 is a mixed respiratory and lactic metabolic acidosis. Potassium 5.8 is high. Glucose 14.8 is high. hs-troponin T 1,850 is markedly raised. Hb 142, platelets and coagulation are normal. WCC 13.4 is mildly raised (stress). Urea 8.6 and creatinine 118 are mildly raised, with no baseline (eGFR is not valid in acute illness). Magnesium and calcium are normal. Group O positive, antibody screen negative.
  • Meaning: the acidosis, lactate, potassium and glucose are the expected picture after 10 minutes of arrest with low flow. The hyperkalaemia is mild (5.8) and fits the acidosis (and the ARB). It is a reversible cause to recheck, not the likely trigger. The troponin is markedly raised, which fits an infarct evolving since 05:30, but reperfusion is decided on the ECG, not the troponin. No anaemia or coagulopathy; with no bleeding source on examination, it is safe to proceed with antithrombotics (Hb lags in acute bleeding, so it does not on its own exclude haemorrhage).
  • Changes: a venous pCO2 in a low-flow shock state is unreliable, so confirm with an arterial blood gas (arterial line) and continuous waveform capnography (EtCO2) before targeting normocapnia. Repeat the gas and potassium within 30 to 60 minutes, treating if it rises or the ECG changes. Treat persistent hyperglycaemia avoiding hypoglycaemia (aim about 6 to 10 mmol/L). Withhold metformin (lactic acidosis, contrast, renal function) and telmisartan (hypotension, potassium).

labs.title: Venous blood gas (10:24, on 15 L/min oxygen)

rows.n: not valid in acute illness; no baseline
about 5 hours after symptom onset; after CPR and defibrillation

ask: You are now calling the interventional cardiology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Phillip Smith, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Phillip now, here in the emergency department, including his transfer to the cath lab.
Helen asks you what has happened and whether Phillip is going to be all right. Please answer her, then tell me what care and follow-up Phillip will need after he leaves the emergency department.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED registrar; Phillip Smith, 75, in ED resus.
  • Situation: witnessed VF arrest at 10:08; 4 shocks and the drugs actually given (with correct ANZCOR timing this is adrenaline 2 mg and amiodarone 300 mg); ROSC 10:18. GCS 3, now BP 82/50, HR 122.
  • Background: breathless since 05:30 with chest tightness and sweating. T2DM, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, ex-smoker; telmisartan, atorvastatin, metformin; no antithrombotics, no bleeding risk; independent, for full treatment.
  • Assessment: abnormal obs before the arrest; after ROSC unresponsive, BP falling to 82 systolic, HR 122: post-arrest shock. ECG anterolateral STEMI, likely proximal LAD. Gas: mixed respiratory and lactic acidosis (pH 7.12, pCO2 58, lactate 8.6), K 5.8, glucose 14.8. Troponin raised; Hb, platelets and coagulation normal.
  • Recommendation: accept for immediate angiography and PCI; advise on antithrombotics; ICU involved.

VF cardiac arrest from an acute anterolateral STEMI (likely proximal LAD): a diabetic man with breathlessness, chest tightness and sweating since 05:30, VF, ST elevation with reciprocal change and Q waves, raised troponin, bibasal crackles.

  • Pulmonary embolism: for: breathless, SpO2 93%. Against: no risk factors, normal calves, territorial ST elevation, VF rather than PEA.
  • Hyperkalaemia: for: K 5.8 on an ARB. Against: mild, explained by the acidosis; recheck.
  • Hypoxia: for: SpO2 93% at triage. Against: mild, from LV failure.
  • Tension pneumothorax or tamponade: against: trachea central, equal air entry, heart sounds not muffled, shocks restored output.
  • Hypovolaemia: no bleeding or fluid loss in the history, no injury from the fall, Hb normal (though Hb lags in acute bleeding). Glucose 14.8.

1. Pads on and continuous monitoring in resus and on transfer, with defibrillator, drugs and an airway-skilled escort; watch for recurrent VF and worsening shock.
  2. Activate the cath lab: immediate angiography and PCI (STEMI after cardiac arrest), with no wait for the troponin; ICU after PCI.
  3. Nothing by mouth while the airway is unprotected; aspirin (via orogastric tube once intubated, or IV if available) and heparin or other antithrombotics agreed with the interventional cardiologist.
  4. Airway: definitive airway; SpO2 94 to 98%; normocapnia confirmed on ABG/EtCO2.
  5. Circulation: vasopressor or inotrope for cardiogenic shock, MAP 65 or above.
  6. Glucose 6 to 10 mmol/L, avoiding hypoglycaemia; withhold metformin.
  7. Prevent fever (37.5 °C or below); do not rewarm.

• To Helen: a heart attack (a blocked heart artery) made his heart stop; the team restarted it; he is going straight for a procedure to open the artery. He is critically ill and it is too early to know how he will recover, including his brain. It was not her fault. Invites her questions, offers her a place near him and a social worker.
  • After ED (a one-sentence list; credit item 41 for naming any three of the four): ICU post-arrest care after PCI; neurological prognosis not before 72 hours; echo and ICD assessment; cardiac rehabilitation.

ddx.dx: Ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest from acute anterolateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction (proximal left anterior descending occlusion)
ddx.for: A diabetic ex-smoker with breathlessness, chest tightness and sweating since 05:30, VF, ST elevation in V2 to V4, I, aVL, V5 and V6 with reciprocal inferior depression and Q waves, and a raised troponin.
He was breathless all day with SpO2 93% and RR 24 at triage before he collapsed.
ddx.against: He has no leg swelling, travel, surgery or previous clot, his rhythm was VF rather than PEA, and the ECG shows territorial ST elevation with reciprocal change.

ddx.for: Potassium is 5.8 in a diabetic man taking an angiotensin receptor blocker.
ddx.against: The rise is mild, fits an acidosis of pH 7.12 after 10 minutes of arrest, and the ECG has no peaked T waves or broad QRS.

ddx.for: He was tachypnoeic and hypoxic at triage with SpO2 93% on room air.
ddx.against: The hypoxia was mild and explained by LV failure (bibasal crackles), and hypoxic arrests usually present as PEA or asystole rather than VF.

ddx.for: He had an evolving anterior infarct (rupture is a late risk) and has had CPR after a fall.
ddx.against: His trachea is central, air entry is equal, heart sounds are not muffled, and defibrillation restored a perfusing rhythm.

guide:
Use a mannequin, with a helper as the nurse and team if possible; otherwise the candidate talks through each step. Compress time: each time the candidate calls for 2 minutes of CPR, say "Two minutes have passed, rhythm check due." Rhythm checks 1 to 4 show VF (show the rhythm strip or read it out). At rhythm check 5, after 4 shocks, ROSC occurs at about minute 6 of the station whatever drugs have been given. That leaves about 4 minutes for the primary survey and Helen's history. From the second rhythm check, Helen stands beside the team leader. Credit any history the team leader takes between rhythm checks. If no history has been started by ROSC, the nurse says "His wife is here if you want to ask her anything." Do not prompt the drugs. Note when adrenaline and amiodarone are ordered and mark items 31 and 32 against ANZCOR timing (adrenaline after the second shock then every second loop, amiodarone after the third shock). Credit history taken from Helen during CPR, as long as the candidate stays the hands-off team leader and the resuscitation is not interrupted.

Accept the defibrillator manufacturer's energy (commonly 150 to 200 J biphasic). Accept a jaw thrust or a head tilt–chin lift; a jaw thrust with manual in-line stabilisation is preferred after a fall. Accept a request for an advanced airway by a skilled operator. If the candidate asks for a 12-lead ECG, bloods or a gas in Part 1, say they are done and given in Part 2; credit the request against items 30 and 33. Treatment ordered in Part 1 counts towards the Management items.

In Part 2, hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order (about 75 seconds each). In the ISBAR, mark the Situation against the drugs this candidate actually gave in Part 1, not a fixed total. In question 4 the examiner or actor speaks as Helen; credit item 41 for any three of the four follow-up elements. Credit oral aspirin being withheld while he is unconscious. Credit aspirin via an orogastric tube or IV, and other antithrombotics, if the candidate says they are agreed with the cardiologist.

A high-performing candidate checks danger, confirms unresponsiveness, calls the arrest and starts good CPR within seconds. They identify VF and shock safely with COACHED, give adrenaline and amiodarone at the right loops, and recognise ROSC. They then ask at once for a 12-lead ECG, survey ABCDE including glucose, and get a focused collateral history including goals of care and bleeding risk. In Part 2 they call an anterolateral STEMI as the cause, read the gas as an expected post-arrest picture, activate the cath lab, and run post-resuscitation care to the ANZCOR targets. They speak to Helen honestly and kindly.

A borderline candidate delays CPR to assess further, pauses compressions for long pulse checks, gets drug timing wrong, or forgets the 12-lead ECG after ROSC. They may call the ECG "ST changes after the shocks" or wait for the troponin, attribute the arrest to the potassium, give oral aspirin to an unconscious patient, or offer Helen false reassurance.
explain:
Diagnosis: VF arrest from an anterolateral STEMI

Phillip had a witnessed collapse in ED after a morning of breathlessness, sweating and chest "tightness" that he called indigestion. Breathlessness alone is a common presentation of acute coronary syndrome in older people and people with diabetes. His first rhythm was ventricular fibrillation (VF). His post-resuscitation ECG shows an anterolateral STEMI: ST elevation in V2 to V4 and the lateral leads I, aVL, V5 and V6, with reciprocal depression in III and aVF. Q waves are most prominent in V2 to V4, which shows that the infarct has been evolving for hours.

VF is a rapid, disorganised arrhythmia. The ventricles contract out of sync, so there is no cardiac output and no recordable blood pressure, and it is fatal unless treated quickly. It most often comes from ischaemic heart disease and acute myocardial ischaemia. Several mechanisms make ischaemic myocardium arrhythmogenic:

  • Substrate: re-entrant circuits and enhanced automaticity in damaged myocardium.
  • Triggers: variations in cycle length and heart rate.
  • Modulating factors: electrolyte imbalance, autonomic dysfunction, continued ischaemia and impaired LV function.

DRSABCD and the team

Check for danger (slip hazards such as spilled water, which also matters for defibrillation, and sharps), put on gloves if they are at hand without delaying anything, and assess response by talk and touch: a simple command and a firm squeeze of the shoulders. Send for help: press the emergency buzzer, call a Code Blue and ask for the defibrillator to be brought to the patient. Apply the pads and check the rhythm where he lies; early defibrillation and minimal interruptions to CPR come first, so move him to the resus bay after ROSC (or only when this will not delay defibrillation or interrupt CPR). Allocate roles:

  • Team leader: communicates, directs, orders investigations, establishes the diagnosis and coordinates management.
  • Airway: keeps the airway patent and ventilates.
  • Circulation: early IV access with two large-bore cannulas (intraosseous if IV fails) and bloods.
  • Defibrillation: pads, COACHED and safety.
  • Scribe: records the times of events, the medicines and the rhythm at each check.
  • Medications: prepares and gives them.

Open the airway, using a jaw thrust with C-spine precautions after a fall, or a head tilt–chin lift. Use suction, a bag-valve-mask with a good seal and chest rise, and an oropharyngeal airway sized from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw. A nasopharyngeal airway, laryngeal mask or endotracheal tube is placed by a skilled operator, and waveform capnography is used once an advanced airway is in place to confirm placement and monitor CPR quality. Check breathing and the pulse for no more than 10 seconds. An unresponsive patient who is not breathing normally needs CPR:

  • Lower half of the sternum, hands interlocked, elbows straight.
  • Rate 100 to 120/min, depth one third of the chest.
  • 30:2 until an advanced airway is placed.
  • Minimal interruptions, swapping compressors every 2 minutes.

Defibrillation and drugs (ANZCOR adult ALS)

The shockable rhythms are VF and pulseless VT. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are non-shockable. Pads go in the anterolateral position, clear of jewellery or a pacemaker, shaving if needed. Shock using COACHED:

  • Continue compressions.
  • Oxygen away.
  • All others clear.
  • Charge (at the device's recommended energy).
  • Hands off.
  • Evaluate the rhythm.
  • Defibrillate, or disarm the charge, keeping your eyes on the patient.

Resume CPR straight away for 2 minutes, then repeat the rhythm check. Give adrenaline 1 mg IV after the second shock and then every second loop (about every 4 minutes). Give amiodarone 300 mg IV after the third shock. Other resuscitation drugs have specific uses:

  • Calcium: hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, calcium-channel blocker overdose (insulin is also used for hyperkalaemia).
  • Lignocaine: if amiodarone is unavailable, or for refractory VF or VT.
  • Magnesium: hypomagnesaemia, torsades de pointes, diuretic use, digoxin toxicity.
  • Sodium bicarbonate: hyperkalaemia, tricyclic or sodium-channel blocker overdose, severe metabolic acidosis.
  • Alteplase: pulmonary embolism.
  • Fluids and blood products: hypovolaemia and haemorrhage.

Reversible causes and investigations

During and after the arrest, look for the 4 Hs and 4 Ts:

  • 4 Hs: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hyper- or hypokalaemia and other metabolic disorders, hypo- or hyperthermia.
  • 4 Ts: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary).

The investigations are:

  • Bedside: vital signs, a 12-lead ECG and point-of-care ultrasound.
  • Bloods: a venous or arterial gas, FBC, UEC, LFT, coagulation, group and hold, and troponin.

After an arrest the gas typically shows a respiratory and metabolic acidosis with a high lactate, hyperkalaemia and hyperglycaemia, as Phillip's does. These are consequences of the arrest. They are rechecked as ventilation and perfusion improve, and are not taken as its cause. Here coronary thrombosis is the cause. A venous pCO2 taken in a low-flow shock state does not reliably reflect arterial CO2, so ventilation is guided by an arterial gas and continuous waveform capnography. A normal haemoglobin minutes after a collapse does not exclude acute bleeding, because Hb lags behind blood loss; the absence of a bleeding source on history and examination is what matters before antithrombotics. eGFR is not valid in acute illness.

An ECG recorded within the first few minutes of ROSC is more likely to show ST change that is not a true STEMI. Phillip's reciprocal change, Q waves and history make a true STEMI far more likely; the 12-lead is repeated about 10 minutes after ROSC and after any rhythm change, without delaying cath lab activation.

After ROSC

Repeat the primary survey (ABCDE, including glucose):

  • Airway and breathing: secure a definitive airway with continuous waveform capnography, aim for SpO2 94 to 98% and normocapnia confirmed on an arterial gas, and get a chest X-ray after intubation.
  • Circulation: look for haemorrhage and shock (pulse, CRT, skin colour, BP), record a 12-lead ECG, and secure IV access and an arterial line. Avoid hypotension, targeting MAP ≥65 mmHg (systolic above 90 to 100).
  • Disability: GCS or AVPU, pupils, glucose ("don't ever forget glucose") and a quick neurological examination.
  • Exposure: allergens, injuries and temperature.

Repeat the investigations and treat the precipitating cause. Aim for normoglycaemia (about 6 to 10 mmol/L, avoiding hypoglycaemia). Temperature control: monitor core temperature continuously and actively prevent fever (keep it at or below 37.5 °C) for at least 72 hours in patients who remain comatose. There is not enough evidence to recommend routine cooling to 32 to 36 °C over active fever prevention; mild post-arrest hypothermia is not actively rewarmed. Maintain cerebral perfusion.

Cardiogenic shock is a systolic BP below 90 mmHg for more than 30 minutes (or needing vasopressors, inotropes or mechanical support to keep it there) with signs of poor perfusion, such as cool peripheries, a long CRT, raised lactate or low urine output. Phillip is heading that way.

Neurological prognosis is not judged in the first 72 hours. Survivors need an echo of LV function, assessment for an ICD where it is indicated, secondary prevention and cardiac rehabilitation.

Reperfusion

A patient resuscitated from cardiac arrest whose ECG shows STEMI goes for immediate coronary angiography and PCI (Heart Foundation and CSANZ Australian ACS guideline 2025). Nothing is given by mouth while the airway is unprotected; aspirin (via orogastric tube once intubated, or IV if available) and heparin or other antithrombotics are agreed with the interventional cardiologist. Metformin and telmisartan are withheld because of the lactic acidosis, contrast, kidney function, hypotension and potassium.

Communication

Families should be supported during a resuscitation, with a staff member assigned to them, and given honest, plain-language updates: what happened, what happens next, and that the outcome is uncertain. Helen's guilt about not bringing him in earlier should be met directly and kindly.

Post-resuscitation detail

  • Venous pCO2 is unreliable in shock: confirm with an arterial blood gas (arterial line) and continuous waveform capnography before targeting normocapnia.
  • Cardiogenic shock: arterial line, cautious fluid, then a vasopressor or inotrope with ICU, targeting MAP 65 mmHg or above (systolic above 90 to 100).
  • Glucose: insulin infusion if persistently above 10 mmol/L; repeat the gas and potassium; withhold metformin and telmisartan (creatinine 118, contrast due).
  • Temperature: continuous core monitoring and active fever prevention for at least 72 hours.
points: Unresponsive and not breathing normally means cardiac arrest: call for help and start CPR at once (lower half of the sternum, 100 to 120/min, one third of chest depth, 30:2, minimal interruptions).
VF and pulseless VT are shockable. Defibrillate with COACHED, resume CPR straight away for 2 minutes, and check the rhythm every 2 minutes.
ANZCOR drugs for shockable rhythms: adrenaline 1 mg IV after the second shock then every second loop, and amiodarone 300 mg IV after the third shock.

Look for the 4 Hs (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hyper- or hypokalaemia and metabolic, hypo- or hyperthermia) and 4 Ts (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis). Acidosis, raised lactate, raised potassium and hyperglycaemia are expected after an arrest.

After ROSC, record a 12-lead ECG straight away. ST elevation means immediate angiography and PCI. Give nothing by mouth while the airway is unprotected; agree aspirin (via orogastric tube or IV) and other antithrombotics with cardiology.

Post-resuscitation care: a definitive airway, SpO2 94 to 98%, normocapnia, avoiding hypotension (MAP ≥65 mmHg), glucose about 6 to 10 mmol/L and temperature control. Do not judge neurological prognosis before 72 hours.
